story877:
In the underworld, the Apache people lived in darkness. Holy Boy was unhappy. He was young and restless, and he wanted to see what light looked like, though no one in the underworld could describe it.

"I will make a sun," Holy Boy declared. He tried many materials — clay, which crumbled. Wood, which burned too quickly. Stone, which was too heavy to lift into the sky. Each attempt failed, and the people told him to stop trying.

But Cyclone, who had eyes that could see through walls and across dimensions, had been spying on the Hactcin. He returned to Holy Boy with news: "White Hactcin has the sun. Black Hactcin has the moon. They keep them hidden because they believe humans are not ready."

Holy Boy went to White Hactcin. "Lend me the sun," he said. "My people suffer in darkness."

White Hactcin studied him for a long time. Then he said, "You are not ready. But I will teach you how to hold it." He showed Holy Boy how to make a sacred sandpainting on a buckskin — a pattern of colored sand so precise and powerful it could contain the sun's energy without being consumed.

Holy Boy went to Black Hactcin and asked for the moon. Black Hactcin agreed, and taught him a second sandpainting, silver and gray, to hold the moon's cooler light.

Holy Boy, Red Boy, Black Hactcin, and White Hactcin held a ceremony. They sang four songs. On the fourth song, White Hactcin released the sun from his bundle, and Black Hactcin released the moon. Light blazed across the sky, so bright that the medicine people shielded their eyes.

But immediately the medicine people began to argue. "I made the sun!" cried one. "No, I did!" shouted another. Their argument grew so loud that it reached the ears of the Hactcin.

"Remember this," the Hactcin warned. "There will come a time when the sun disappears. You will think it has been stolen. Do not claim you can bring it back. Only the Hactcin can restore it."

When the first eclipse came, the medicine people panicked. They performed ceremonies, shouted spells, burned sacred herbs. The sun did not return. Only when the Hactcin sang their songs did the light reappear.

The story teaches Apache children that humans should never claim divine powers, and that some forces in the universe are beyond human control.
story878:
After the Apaches emerged from the underworld, they traveled south for four days with nothing to eat but seeds. The children cried from hunger. The elders walked slowly, their steps weighted by emptiness.

Then a Raven appeared, carrying a quiver full of meat on its back. It flew to a teepee and dropped the quiver at the door. The children fell upon the meat, eating greedily, and within moments they were fat — their bellies round, their cheeks full, their laughter returning.

But the meat was stolen. Someone took the Raven's quiver while the bird was searching for more food. The Raven, discovering the theft, flew to his home on the eastern mountain, his cries of outrage echoing across the plains.

An Apache boy volunteered to follow. The spirits transformed him into a puppy — small, brown, unremarkable — so he could sneak into the Raven's camp without suspicion. Hidden among the young ravens, the puppy watched as an old raven removed a flat stone from the ground, revealing an opening to the underworld beneath.

Each evening, a buffalo emerged from the opening. The ravens surrounded it and ate. The puppy watched for four days, memorizing the pattern, the timing, the weakness in the ravens' guard.

On the fourth night, the boy resumed his human shape. He descended into the underworld carrying white and black feathers as talismans. There, in the vast cavern, he found the buffalo — a great herd, grazing in the eternal darkness.

"Come with me," the boy told the buffalo. "The people are hungry. They will honor you and remember you in their ceremonies."

The buffalo agreed, and they followed the boy to the Apache camp. All the animals came too — deer, elk, antelope — for the boy had spoken with authority and the animals trusted him.

But an old grandmother, sitting by the fire, saw a deer approaching too close. She struck its nose with a fire stick, leaving a white mark. "From now on," she decreed, "animals will avoid humans. They will use their noses to detect us from afar."

And so the harmony between humans and animals ended. The deer still carries the white mark on its nose, a reminder of the moment when the easy intimacy between species was broken by a single, irrevocable act.
story879:
The Gahe — the Mountain Spirits — are among the most powerful supernatural beings in Apache tradition. They live inside the sacred mountains, hidden in caves of crystal and stone, and they emerge only when the people call them with the proper songs and offerings.

The first Mountain Spirit ceremony was taught to the Apache by the children of the Sun, who descended from the sky world carrying masks and rattles and the knowledge of how to summon the Gahe. The ceremony was part of the Girls' Puberty Ceremony — the Sunrise Ceremony — the longest and most sacred ritual in Apache life.

When the Gahe appear, they wear distinctive tall headdresses made of wooden slats painted black and white, arranged in patterns that represent the mountains themselves. Their bodies are painted with black and white designs — zigzags for lightning, circles for rain, lines for the paths the spirits travel between the mountain and the sky. They wear black buckskin kilts and carry spruce boughs.

Four Mountain Spirits dance together — one for each cardinal direction: East, South, West, North. Each carries the power of its direction. The eastern spirit brings the light of dawn and the promise of new beginnings. The southern spirit brings the warmth of midday and the power of growth. The western spirit brings the twilight and the wisdom of endings. The northern spirit brings the cold and the strength of endurance.

A clown figure dances with them, interrupting the solemn ceremony with comic gestures and absurd behavior. The clown serves a dual purpose — to remind the people not to take themselves too seriously, and to distract any malevolent spirits that might be lurking nearby.

The dancers move in a syncopated, swaying rhythm to the sound of singing and drumming. They trace sacred patterns on the dance ground with their feet, pressing designs into the dirt that mirror the patterns painted on their bodies.

The Gahe possess healing powers. They can cure illness, drive away evil influences, and bring blessings to the young woman undergoing her transformation into adulthood. When the ceremony is complete, the masks are returned to the mountain, for they are not costumes but faces — the Gahe's own faces, temporarily lent to human dancers.

Sierra Blanca — the White Mountain in New Mexico — is considered the spiritual origin place of many Mountain Spirit dance groups. It is from this mountain that the first Gahe emerged, and it is to this mountain that they return when the ceremony ends.
